blocks.text: Model export converts a trained or merged model, covered in the previous Adapter Merging topic, from its training-time format into a format suitable for a specific deployment target, a necessary step before serving through frameworks like vLLM, Ollama, TensorRT-LLM, or TGI, all covered in the topics that follow.
This topic covers the common export formats and what each is optimized for, the security consideration around pickle-based formats, and how to validate that an exported model still behaves correctly.
1. Why Export Is a Distinct Step

blocks.alt: A training format goes through model export, producing a deployment format

blocks.text: The format a model is saved in immediately after training is not always the ideal format for serving it in production, export converts between these representations, sometimes changing precision, sometimes changing the underlying file structure entirely, to match what a specific serving framework expects.
2. Common Export Formats

blocks.alt: SafeTensors, ONNX, GGUF, and TensorRT engine are common export formats

blocks.text: SafeTensors is a safe, efficient format for storing model weights, ONNX is a cross-framework computation graph format, GGUF is optimized for efficient CPU and consumer hardware inference, commonly used with Ollama covered in a later topic, and a TensorRT engine is a highly optimized, hardware-specific format for NVIDIA GPUs, each format trades generality for a specific deployment advantage.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Format","Optimized For"],"rows":[["SafeTensors","Safe, efficient weight storage, widely compatible"],["ONNX","Cross-framework portability"],["GGUF","Efficient CPU and consumer hardware inference"],["TensorRT engine","Maximum performance on specific NVIDIA GPU hardware"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why SafeTensors Replaced Pickle-Based Formats

blocks.alt: A pickle based format carries security risk while SafeTensors is safe with no code execution

blocks.text: Older PyTorch checkpoint formats rely on Python pickle serialization, which can execute arbitrary code when loading a malicious file, SafeTensors was specifically designed to store only tensor data with no code execution capability, making it the safer default choice for sharing and deploying model weights.

blocks.title: This is a genuine security consideration, not just a technical preference
blocks.content: Loading a pickle-based checkpoint from an untrusted source carries real code execution risk, SafeTensors removes this attack surface entirely by design, which is why most model hubs now default to it.

blocks.text: 4. Converting to ONNX for Cross-Framework Portability

blocks.alt: A PyTorch computation graph converts to a portable cross-framework graph through ONNX

blocks.text: ONNX conversion traces a model computation graph, covered in earlier modules as the sequence of operations a model performs, into a standardized, portable representation, letting the exported model run in a different framework or runtime than the one it was originally trained in.

code.content:
import torch

torch.onnx.export(
    model,
    dummy_input,
    "model.onnx",
    opset_version=17,
    input_names=["input_ids"],
    output_names=["logits"],
)

blocks.text: 5. Full Precision vs Quantized Export

blocks.alt: Full precision export is compared against quantized export

blocks.text: A model can be exported at its original training precision or converted to a quantized format, covered in an earlier module, during the export step itself, quantized export produces a smaller, faster model at the cost of a small accuracy tradeoff, the right choice depends on the target hardware and latency requirements of the deployment.
6. Matching Export Format to Serving Framework

blocks.alt: The target serving framework determines whether to export SafeTensors, GGUF, or a TensorRT engine

blocks.text: Each serving framework covered in the following topics of this module expects a specific format, vLLM commonly works with SafeTensors, Ollama commonly works with GGUF, TensorRT-LLM requires a compiled TensorRT engine, choosing the export format correctly upfront avoids a wasted conversion step later.
7. Validating an Exported Model

blocks.alt: An exported model goes through a validation check confirming it matches original outputs

blocks.text: After exporting, running a validation pass, comparing the exported model outputs against the original model outputs on a fixed set of test inputs, catches conversion errors before they reach production, a silent numerical mismatch introduced during export can otherwise go unnoticed until a subtle quality regression shows up.
8. Export as Part of a Larger Deployment Pipeline

Model export typically sits between the training and evaluation stages covered throughout this course and the actual serving stage, covered in the following topics, a well structured deployment pipeline automates this conversion step consistently rather than treating it as a manual, error-prone one-off task.
9. Keeping Export Configuration Reproducible

Recording exactly which export format, precision, and conversion settings were used for a given deployed model, similar in spirit to the reproducibility goals covered in the earlier Axolotl topic, makes it possible to regenerate an identical deployment artifact later, or to diagnose a production issue back to a specific export configuration.
Worked Example

A team finishes training and merging their fine-tuned model and needs to deploy it through vLLM for high-throughput serving. They export the merged model to SafeTensors format at full precision, matching what vLLM expects.

Before deploying, they run a validation pass comparing outputs from the exported SafeTensors model against their original training-time checkpoint on a fixed evaluation set, confirming outputs match closely enough to proceed, catching this kind of mismatch before production is far cheaper than discovering it after deployment.
Common Mistakes

items: Exporting to a format that does not match what the target serving framework actually expects
Skipping validation after export, missing a silent numerical mismatch introduced during conversion
Using an older pickle-based checkpoint format when SafeTensors is available and safer
Not recording the exact export configuration used, making a deployed artifact hard to reproduce or debug later

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuned model you are deploying or could imagine deploying, identify which serving framework from this module you would target, and based on the matching covered in this topic, decide which export format, SafeTensors, GGUF, or a TensorRT engine, that choice implies.
Key Takeaway

Model export converts a trained model into the specific format a target serving framework expects, SafeTensors, ONNX, GGUF, or a TensorRT engine each optimized for a different deployment scenario, with SafeTensors preferred over older pickle-based formats for its safety, and validating exported model outputs against the original before deployment catches conversion errors that would otherwise surface as hard-to-diagnose production issues.
